name: Software Carbon Intensity (SCI)

foundation.via: Written by the GSF’s Software Standards Working Group; published as ISO/IEC 21031:2024

license: Specification text under CC BY 4.0, developed under the W3C Patent Policy patent mode; also published by ISO and IEC as ISO/IEC 21031:2024
summary: A method for scoring software by its carbon emissions per unit of work, such as grams of CO2e per API call, counting the energy it uses, the grid that powers it and a share of the hardware it runs on.
intro: The SCI is a formula, not a tool: SCI = ((E × I) + M) per R. E is the energy the software uses, in kWh, including the overhead of the data centre, such as cooling, through its PUE. I is the carbon intensity of the electricity, in gCO2e per kWh, taken from the regional grid where it runs. M is the share of the hardware’s embodied emissions, from manufacturing to disposal, allocated to the software by how long and how much of the machine it reserves. R is the functional unit you choose, such as an API call, a user, a transaction or a minute of video, so the result is a rate rather than a total. The boundary has to include everything that significantly supports the software: compute, storage, networking, idle and standby machines, logging and monitoring, build pipelines, backups and, where relevant, end-user devices.

Two rules set it apart from a corporate carbon report. It counts only location-based grid intensity and excludes market-based measures such as renewable energy certificates, power purchase agreements and offsets, so the only way to lower a score is to use less energy, run on a cleaner grid or use less hardware. And because it is a rate, a growing product can still show progress. The Green Software Foundation published version 1.0 in November 2022; ISO and IEC published it as ISO/IEC 21031:2024, and the GSF’s own text is at 1.1.0. Extensions apply it to particular kinds of software: SCI for AI was ratified in 2025, and SCI for Web was a draft in October 2026.
strengths: An ISO/IEC standard, so a score can be explained to auditors, customers and procurement with a public reference
A rate per unit of work, which shows whether each request or user gets cleaner even as traffic grows
Counts embodied hardware emissions, which rewards using fewer and longer-lived machines, not only cleaner electricity
Ignores certificates and offsets, so the score responds only to engineering changes
limits: You choose the boundary and the functional unit, so two products’ scores are rarely comparable; it is built for tracking one system over time
It says what to measure, not how: energy per workload and embodied emissions are hard to get in a public cloud, and most teams end up with estimates
Location-based numbers differ from the market-based figures in many corporate sustainability reports, which can confuse readers

snippet.title: An SCI score for one hour of an API service (illustrative numbers)
source: # E: energy for the hour, with data centre overhead (PUE)
# I: location-based grid intensity of the region, gCO2e per kWh
# M = TE x (TiR / EL) x (RR / ToR): share of the server's embodied carbon
TE = 1_200_000                                  # gCO2e to make the server
M = TE * (hours / EL) * (1 / 1)                 # whole server reserved: ~34 g
# R: functional unit, here API calls served in the hour

sections.title: The four terms
sections.intro: Every component inside the boundary is scored with the same functional unit, and the components are added up.

rows.label: E, energy
values: kWh used by the software per unit of work, counting all hardware reserved or provisioned for it, not only what it keeps busy
Real-world measurement, or a model built in a lab or from supplier data when measurement isn’t possible; data-centre overhead added through its PUE

rows.label: I, carbon intensity
values: gCO2e per kWh of the grid where the energy is used: short-run marginal, long-run marginal or average, but always location-based
Data for the regional grid; an emissions factor for the system itself when it isn’t grid-connected

rows.label: M, embodied emissions
values: TE × (time reserved ÷ expected life) × (resources reserved ÷ total resources)
Life-cycle assessments (LCAs) of the hardware, ideally per device, or simpler estimation models; in the cloud, the share of vCPUs reserved is a suggested resource share

rows.label: R, functional unit
values: What the score is divided by: API call, user, device, transaction, minute
Your own traffic metrics; it should be how the software scales

story: The Green Software Foundation formed its Software Standards Working Group in 2021, its first year, to agree on how to measure software emissions. The aim was a score engineers could move by changing code and infrastructure, rather than a total that certificates and offsets could lower. An alpha of the SCI came out in December 2021.

After public comment, version 1.0 removed ambiguities, for example by settling on location-based emissions factors and saying how to treat data-centre energy, and was announced at the GSF’s Decarbonize Software event during COP27 in November 2022. Navveen Balani of Accenture and Henry Richardson of WattTime led the work. The foundation then took it through ISO/IEC JTC 1, and in 2024 it was published as ISO/IEC 21031:2024. The GSF released version 1.1 of its own text in October 2024.

The method then branched out. Impact Framework, a GSF tool for computing SCI scores from manifests of observations, graduated in 2024, and SCI for AI, led by Balani and Richardson, was ratified in 2025 to cover model training and inference. In 2026 the foundation was also working on energy and water intensity specifications built on the same pattern.

choices.why: A total grows with the business and punishes success. Dividing by a unit of work lets a team show that each request got cleaner, which is what engineering can control.
Market-based figures fall when a company buys certificates, whatever the software does. The SCI excludes them so the score reflects the grid the software actually draws on.
Making servers, phones and network gear causes a large share of IT’s footprint, so the SCI rewards keeping hardware busy and in service for longer, not only buying cleaner electricity.
An international standard gives buyers, auditors and regulators a reference they recognise, which a foundation document alone would not.
